name: King's Gambit, Muzio Gambit
summary: The Muzio Gambit is a fiery King's Gambit line where White sacrifices a whole knight on f3 for a blazing lead in development and attack.
intro: Reached after 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-O gxf3 6.Qxf3, the Muzio Gambit sees White give up the f3-knight outright. In return White gains rapid development, the open f-file, and ferocious pressure against f7 while Black's king lingers in the centre.
line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 O-O gxf3 Qxf3

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: White's compensation is entirely dynamic. The queen sits actively on f3, the bishop rakes f7 from c4, and the rook on f1 bears down the half-open f-file, so every White piece points at Black's fragile kingside. The extra pawn on f4 also cramps Black and shields future attacking pieces.

Black, a full piece to the good, must survive the opening storm and reach an endgame where the material tells. The defensive challenge is enormous: returning some material to blunt the attack, completing development, and getting the king to safety are all more valuable than clinging to the extra piece.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The critical defence is 6...Qf6, defending f7 and offering to trade queens to douse the initiative; White typically continues 7.e5 Qxe5 8.Bxf7+ or 8.d3, keeping the attack alive. The alternative 6...Qe7 is more solid but passive, allowing White easy development with d4 and Nc3.

If Black greedily grabs further material with ...Qxc4 or ...Qxd4, the game can transpose into the Double Muzio, where White sacrifices a second piece for an even more overwhelming attack. These lines are extremely sharp and reward precise home preparation from both sides.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The gambit epitomises the romantic era of the 1800s, when a swashbuckling attack was prized above material. Its name traces to seventeenth-century Italian analysis: the line is associated with Mutio d'Allessandro and was published by Alessandro Salvio, and it later became a favourite testing ground for attacking players and correspondence theorists.

keyIdeas: Sacrifice the f3-knight for a lead in development and open lines
Exploit the open f-file with the rook against f7
Keep the queen active on f3 pressuring f7 and the centre
Use the Bc4 to hammer the f7 square
Delay Black's king from reaching safety
Consider a second sacrifice (Double Muzio) if Black overreaches

white: Complete development quickly with Nc3, d3 or d4, and Bxf4
Open the position further with e5 or d4 to expose the black king
Pile up on the f-file and target f7
Bring the queen and both bishops into the attack before Black castles
Sacrifice more material in Double Muzio style when it accelerates the assault
black: Defend f7 with ...Qf6 or ...Qe7 and offer to trade queens
Return material at the right moment to defuse the initiative
Get the king out of the centre as soon as it is safe
Aim for a queen trade or simplification to reach a winning endgame
